collection: TOEFL iBT 2026 original academic talk practice
note: Three original academic talks of 100–250 words, with four questions each. Requires supervised live delivery. Keep scripts, answers and explanations out of learner view.
examinerInstructions: Read each talk at a natural pace, then present its four questions and four written choices per question. Learners may take notes. Award one classroom practice point per correct answer. These points have no TOEFL scale conversion.

listeningSets.title: Opportunity cost
listeningSets.examinerScript: Imagine that a student has a free afternoon and two realistic choices: attend a photography workshop or complete a paid translation job. If she chooses the workshop, the money she could have earned is part of what she gives up. Economists call the value of the best alternative forgone the opportunity cost of a decision. This cost does not have to be a payment. It can be time or another benefit that would otherwise have been available. Now suppose the student also considered visiting a friend. We do not add the value of every rejected possibility together. Opportunity cost concerns the best alternative she would actually have chosen instead. This distinction matters because resources are limited. A university that uses a room for storage cannot use that same room for a seminar at the same time. Recognising the alternative use helps decision makers compare choices more carefully, even when no money changes hands.

listeningSets.title: Map simplification
listeningSets.examinerScript: A map cannot show every feature of the place it represents. If it did, small details would compete with the information a user actually needs. Mapmakers therefore select and simplify. Think about a diagram of a city’s rail network. The stations may be spaced evenly on the page even though the real distances between them vary. The diagram can still be useful because its main job is to show the order of stops and the connections between lines. It would be a poor choice, however, for estimating the time needed to walk between two stations. A street map may serve that purpose better. So simplification is not automatically a defect. Its value depends on the task. The important question is whether the features preserved by the map match the user’s needs. Reading a map well involves noticing both what it shows and what its design leaves out.

listeningSets.title: Controlled comparison
listeningSets.examinerScript: Suppose a class wants to find out whether a new type of paper towel absorbs more water than the type it normally uses. The students could test both, but a comparison would be hard to interpret if one sample were much larger than the other. They need equal-sized pieces and a consistent testing method. For instance, they might measure how much water each piece absorbs under the same conditions. Keeping other relevant factors constant makes it easier to examine the factor of interest: the towel type. Repeating the test also matters. A single result may be affected by an accidental spill or a reading error. Several trials can reveal whether a pattern is consistent. Even then, the conclusion should stay within the evidence. Testing two brands in one classroom does not prove that one will perform better in every situation. A careful report describes both the result and the conditions under which it was obtained.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How to earn money through photography.
How the best rejected alternative helps explain a decision’s cost.
Why universities should charge for storage rooms.
Why students should avoid taking paid work.
questions.answer: How the best rejected alternative helps explain a decision’s cost.
questions.explanation: The talk defines opportunity cost and illustrates it through alternative uses of time and space.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Why does the speaker describe the student’s free afternoon?
options: To show that photography is more valuable than translation.
To explain how translation fees are calculated.
To illustrate a benefit given up when one option is selected.
To recommend a workshop to new students.
questions.answer: To illustrate a benefit given up when one option is selected.
questions.explanation: The student’s choice introduces the lost benefit of the best alternative.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: According to the speaker, which rejected possibilities count toward opportunity cost?
options: Only the best alternative that would otherwise have been chosen.
Every option that was briefly considered.
Only alternatives involving a direct payment.
Only activities that take place in university rooms.
questions.answer: Only the best alternative that would otherwise have been chosen.
questions.explanation: The lecturer explicitly excludes adding all rejected options together.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: What does the room example imply about a decision with no direct payment?
options: It can never involve a meaningful cost.
It must produce the same benefit for every user.
It removes the need to compare alternatives.
It can still involve giving up another valuable use.
questions.answer: It can still involve giving up another valuable use.
questions.explanation: Using a room for storage prevents a simultaneous seminar even without a monetary transaction.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the speaker’s central point about maps?
options: A useful map must include every physical feature.
Rail diagrams should always show walking distances.
Simplification can help when it suits the map’s purpose.
Street maps are unnecessary in large cities.
questions.answer: Simplification can help when it suits the map’s purpose.
questions.explanation: The talk links useful simplification to the user’s task.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: What information does the rail diagram mainly preserve?
options: The order of stations and connections between lines.
The exact distances between all stations.
The width of every street in the city.
The time taken by each individual passenger.
questions.answer: The order of stations and connections between lines.
questions.explanation: The speaker identifies stop order and line connections as the diagram’s main information.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Why does the speaker mention a street map?
options: To argue that rail travel is unreliable.
To show a map that may be better for a different task.
To claim that station names should be removed.
To explain why all maps use equal spacing.
questions.answer: To show a map that may be better for a different task.
questions.explanation: A street map is contrasted with the rail diagram for estimating walking journeys.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: What should a person do before using a map for a particular journey?
options: Assume every gap represents the same distance.
Ignore the information omitted by the designer.
Choose the map with the largest number of colours.
Check whether its design supports the intended task.
questions.answer: Check whether its design supports the intended task.
questions.explanation: The conclusion asks readers to relate the map’s preserved features to their needs.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: What is the speaker mainly explaining through the paper-towel example?
options: Why all classroom products should be replaced.
How towel manufacturers set prices.
Why students should avoid using water in experiments.
How to make a comparison easier to interpret.
questions.answer: How to make a comparison easier to interpret.
questions.explanation: The speaker explains controlled conditions, repetition and limits on conclusions.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Why should the students use equal-sized towel pieces?
options: To make the towels appear equally attractive.
To prevent sample size from obscuring the effect of towel type.
To avoid measuring any absorbed water.
To ensure that both brands produce identical results.
questions.answer: To prevent sample size from obscuring the effect of towel type.
questions.explanation: A size difference could influence absorption and confuse the intended comparison.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Why does the speaker recommend several trials?
options: To guarantee that the new brand wins.
To replace the need for a consistent method.
To check whether the pattern survives accidental variation.
To make the samples increase in size each time.
questions.answer: To check whether the pattern survives accidental variation.
questions.explanation: Repeated trials help reveal whether a result is consistent rather than accidental.

questions.subject: Listening
questions.learningObjective: Interpret main ideas, details, organisation and inferences in a short academic talk.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion would fit the speaker’s advice?
options: One towel absorbed more under the stated test conditions.
One towel will be best in every possible situation.
All paper towels absorb exactly the same amount.
A single spill proves that the method cannot work.
questions.answer: One towel absorbed more under the stated test conditions.
questions.explanation: The conclusion should describe the observed result and its conditions without universal claims.
